articles.title: Keeping a private index of vaccination records
articles.summary: Help a household locate official vaccination records without guessing immunisation status.

visual.alt: A compact three-row offline checklist labelled Record, Location, Review. It organises administrative information only and does not depict a clinical procedure.
visual.caption: A private information-finding aid, not clinical instructions.

sections.title: Identify the original record
paragraphs: Record where an NHS app entry, clinic document or personal health record can be found, including the provider and the date shown. A handwritten list is a finding aid, not proof that a vaccine was administered or protection is current.
Avoid copying sensitive identifiers into shared notes. If entries disagree or are missing, ask the relevant healthcare service to clarify rather than filling gaps from memory.

sections.title: Make a compact index
paragraphs: List the document type, who controls access, and where the authoritative record can be retrieved. Distinguish the date of the vaccination from the date you last checked the record.
Keep the index private and accessible only to the person concerned or someone they authorise. Do not assume that one record contains every vaccination given by different providers.

sections.title: Review when circumstances change
paragraphs: Update the index after receiving a new official record or changing healthcare providers. For travel, school or employment evidence, check the actual requirements with the requesting organisation.
This guide does not recommend a vaccine schedule or determine immunity; clinical advice must come from a qualified professional.

articles.title: Tracking a healthcare referral without losing the original details
articles.summary: Organise a referral status note while avoiding assumptions about waiting times or clinical priority.

visual.alt: A compact three-row offline checklist labelled Referral, Status, Contact. It organises administrative information only and does not depict a clinical procedure.
visual.caption: A private information-finding aid, not clinical instructions.

sections.title: Identify the referral
paragraphs: Keep the referring service, destination service, date of referral and any reference number together. Record only information supplied by the provider; a request being sent does not always mean an appointment is booked.
Keep copies of relevant letters or messages in a private location and preserve their dates. Avoid including diagnostic information in shared household calendars.

sections.title: Track what is confirmed
paragraphs: Separate 'referred', 'acknowledged', 'appointment offered' and 'attended' so the record does not imply a stage has happened prematurely. Note which service to contact about administrative queries.
If an expected message has not arrived, use the service's published contact method to ask about status. Do not invent waiting-time deadlines or interpret delays as evidence of clinical safety.

sections.title: Respond to changing needs
paragraphs: A referral tracker is not a substitute for clinical assessment. If symptoms worsen or new urgent symptoms develop, seek appropriate medical advice rather than waiting for a routine appointment.
Retire outdated contact information and close the note once the referral has been resolved.

articles.title: Organising hospital discharge information for later reference
articles.summary: Keep the official discharge documents findable without replacing personalised instructions.

visual.alt: A compact three-row offline checklist labelled Documents, Contacts, Follow-up. It organises administrative information only and does not depict a clinical procedure.
visual.caption: A private information-finding aid, not clinical instructions.

sections.title: Preserve the original instructions
paragraphs: After a hospital visit, keep the discharge summary and any separate medicine, follow-up or equipment instructions together. Check that the documents belong to the correct person and visit.
If instructions are unclear, missing or appear contradictory, ask the discharging service or appropriate clinician to clarify. Do not rewrite clinical directions from memory.

sections.title: Make a retrieval index
paragraphs: Create a short note showing where the original paperwork is stored, which service issued it and any follow-up contact information. Mark the date and keep later corrections alongside the original rather than silently replacing it.
Do not turn a general household checklist into a treatment plan. Individual medicine changes, restrictions and warning signs must come from the person's own clinical instructions.

sections.title: Protect privacy and continuity
paragraphs: Share documents only with the patient or people authorised to assist. Avoid leaving sensitive details on a communal noticeboard or unlocked device.
If a new urgent concern develops after discharge, seek appropriate professional help instead of assuming the original paperwork covers every possible change.

articles.title: Keeping hearing-aid model and support information together
articles.summary: Make everyday hearing support easier to maintain without improvising device repairs.

visual.alt: A compact three-row offline checklist labelled Device, Supplies, Support. It organises administrative information only and does not depict a clinical procedure.
visual.caption: A private information-finding aid, not clinical instructions.

sections.title: Identify the equipment
paragraphs: Record the hearing-aid make, model and provider contact details from the original documentation. Keep the manufacturer's instructions and any charging or battery compatibility information easy to find.
Different models use different consumables and cleaning arrangements. Do not substitute batteries or dismantle the device based on a generic guide.

sections.title: Organise everyday support
paragraphs: Keep an appropriate labelled case and approved accessories together in a dry, accessible place. Note where replacement consumables can be obtained and whether the person prefers written, visual or spoken communication.
Avoid storing small batteries where children or pets can reach them. A swallowed button battery is an emergency requiring immediate professional advice.

sections.title: Plan for service interruptions
paragraphs: Write down how to contact the fitting service or manufacturer for faults, lost devices or adjustments. A device that stops working may create important communication barriers during a disruption.
Ask the wearer what support is useful rather than assuming their communication preferences.

articles.title: Preparing a short question card for a healthcare appointment
articles.summary: Help a person explain priorities and remember answers without turning notes into medical advice.

visual.alt: A compact three-row offline checklist labelled Questions, Answers, Next step. It organises administrative information only and does not depict a clinical procedure.
visual.caption: A private information-finding aid, not clinical instructions.

sections.title: Choose the main questions
paragraphs: Before a routine appointment, write two or three questions in the person's own words. Include what they most want to understand, such as the purpose of a test or how to obtain a copy of instructions.
Leave room for the clinician's answer and for uncertainties. Avoid collecting more personal details than the person wants to share.

sections.title: Make the card accessible
paragraphs: Use readable type, generous spacing and plain language. A paper card or offline note can be helpful when phone signal, battery or concentration is limited.
Ask whether a companion, interpreter or accessible format would help; the patient should control what is shared and who attends.

sections.title: Check understanding afterward
paragraphs: Record any agreed next step using the professional's wording, and ask for written information when useful. If something remains unclear, contact the relevant service for clarification rather than guessing.
Do not treat the card as a prescription, diagnosis or substitute for a clinical record.

articles.title: Creating an offline index of home medical device manuals
articles.summary: Keep model-specific instructions accessible when an internet connection is unavailable.

visual.alt: A compact three-row offline checklist labelled Model, Manual, Support. It organises administrative information only and does not depict a clinical procedure.
visual.caption: A private information-finding aid, not clinical instructions.

sections.title: Identify each device precisely
paragraphs: Record the manufacturer's model name and the location of its original manual for equipment already used in the household. Include a service contact and the date the manual was obtained.
Avoid placing serial numbers, account details or health information in public repository files or shared templates. Model differences can make a generic instruction unsafe.

sections.title: Keep an offline reference
paragraphs: Where permitted, save a legitimate copy of the correct manual locally or keep the printed instructions with the device. Check that the manual matches the exact model and language needs.
An offline manual can become outdated; retain revision details and check for official safety notices when connectivity is available.

sections.title: Know the limits
paragraphs: Do not attempt repairs, calibration, settings changes or treatment adjustments using this general index. Contact the device provider for faults and follow the individual's clinical plan.
If failure of essential equipment creates an immediate health emergency, seek emergency assistance.

articles.title: Distinguishing current and older personal care plans
articles.summary: Prevent confusion between outdated and current clinician-issued care documents.

visual.alt: A compact three-row offline checklist labelled Source, Version, Confirm. It organises administrative information only and does not depict a clinical procedure.
visual.caption: A private information-finding aid, not clinical instructions.

sections.title: Identify the issuing source
paragraphs: A household may hold several versions of a care plan after appointments or changes in services. Record the document's date, issuing clinician or service and any explicit revision identifier.
Do not assume the newest file timestamp makes a plan clinically current; confirm with the responsible healthcare professional if documents conflict.

sections.title: Keep versions clearly separated
paragraphs: Store the plan believed current where authorised carers can find it, and label older copies as superseded only when a responsible professional has confirmed the replacement.
Preserve necessary historical records securely rather than destroying them casually. Keep personal details out of public or communal lists.

sections.title: Confirm before acting
paragraphs: If an instruction is ambiguous or inconsistent, contact the relevant care team. Do not combine sections from different plans or infer new medication instructions.
Review access permissions when a helper changes, and keep a simple record of when the index was last checked.

articles.title: Recording communication preferences for healthcare conversations
articles.summary: Make consent-based communication support findable in stressful or disrupted situations.

visual.alt: A compact three-row offline checklist labelled Preference, Format, Consent. It organises administrative information only and does not depict a clinical procedure.
visual.caption: A private information-finding aid, not clinical instructions.

sections.title: Ask rather than assume
paragraphs: With the person's agreement, record whether they prefer large print, written explanations, a qualified interpreter, hearing support or another accessible communication method.
Communication needs can vary by setting and over time. Avoid assigning a diagnosis or assuming that a companion can interpret confidential clinical information.

sections.title: Create a minimal preference card
paragraphs: Use a few short, practical phrases about preferred formats and how to request support from the healthcare service. Keep the card separate from unnecessary medical details.
If the person uses an assistive communication tool, note where it is kept and how to request help with it, without storing passwords or private identifiers.

sections.title: Keep control with the person
paragraphs: Ask permission before sharing the card, and let the person update or withdraw preferences. Check that the chosen format remains usable offline if mobile connectivity fails.
The card does not replace a healthcare provider's duty to assess communication and consent needs.
